```{r setup}
library(treatseqr)
```

# Introduction

This vignette uses the initial dataset from the vignette called
`fixed-duration-tunnels.Rmd`, which you can see using
`vignette("fixed-duration-tunnels", package = "treatseqr")`. It then generates
random numbers which still follow "the rules" (i.e., summing to 1) en mass for
use in a probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA). The PSA is then run and the
`ggplot2` trace includes credible intervals (CrIs) for each trace.

As with the `fixed-duration-tunnels.Rmd`, the five model states are:

| State | Type | Tunnel length |
|---|---|---|
| `on_trt` | Pre-tunnel | — |
| `surgery` | Fixed-duration tunnel | 3 cycles |
| `failed_surg` | Fixed-duration tunnel (holding state) | 2 cycles |
| `responder` | Full-length tunnel | `th` cycles |
| `palliative` | Full-length tunnel | `th` cycles |


# Model specification

In a PSA setting the specification is exactly the same:

```{r specify_m}
th <- 20L

m_spec <- specify_m(
  tunnel_lengths    = c(3L, 2L, th, th),
  pre_tunnel_states = 1L
)

m_spec$matrix_size
```

The total matrix size is `r m_spec$matrix_size`: 1 pre-tunnel state + 3 + 2 +
20 + 20 tunnel cycles + 1 death state.

# Transition probabilities

The transition probability source list must follow the standard `treatseqr`
conventions: states listed in sequence order; each state contains transition
probability vectors to all other states (or `NULL`/omit for structural zeros).
With variable-length tunnels, each vector must match the length of the
**source** state's tunnel (or the pre-tunnel horizon `th` for `on_trt`).

In keeping with `fixed-duration-tunnels.Rmd`, the transitions are very simple.
In a "real model", the user of `treatseqr` needs to make their own way of
reliably generating transition probabilities in a probabilistic setting. Because
this can considerably vary from model to model, it is outside the scope of the
package and should be left up to you, the modeller. Usually in `R` there will
be a way to do this, and we cover the most common approach (multivariate normal
draws) below. The key is to make sure that the transition probabilities sum to 1
and converge on the deterministic values you would use in a base-case analysis.

For instance, if you are using Kaplan-Meier (KM) for first line, followed by external
digitized KM data for subsequent lines (what we anticipate to be the most common
use case for this package), we would advise to do the following:

1. Fit parametric survival models to the KM data for each line of therapy, using
   `flexsurv`, `survextrap`, `cuRe`, `rstpm2` and so on.
2. Get the parameters from the fitted models, including the uncertainty taking
   covariance into account (e.g., variance-covariance matrix from `flexsurv`,
others where appropriate). Make sure you know how these are transformed when
provided to you (sometimes you will need to do some maths on paper for this.
Make sure to document it in the function you write to "convert" it to the form
you will use the for the PSA).
3. use random uniform draws (i.e., `runif()`) to generate streams of random
   numbers, and develop a function to take random draws of parameters. The
simplest example is `mvtnorm::rmvnorm()` for simple models that just need a set
of parameters that are correlated. Note that this incorporates the random number
draws as well so you have less than ideal control and have to be careful about
the random seed. Often, one can get into a situation whereby the random
stream can more easily be conserved by pre-drawing the uniform draws and then
feeding that into a similar function of your own making. Note that you can look
at the source code for `mvtnorm::rmvnorm()` to see the more familiar "chol"
method, which is quite simple to implement in an efficient way. This boils down
to the below. Note that you can store the `chol()` ahead of time so you don't
need to calculate it thousands of times, just once per PSA:

```{r mvnorm_draws}
set.seed(12938)
n_illus <- 1000
mu_illus <- c(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3)
sigma_illus <- matrix(c(
  1, 0.5, 0.3,
  0.5, 1, 0.2,
  0.3, 0.2, 1
), nrow = 3)
# This is a fix for near singular matrices, which can happen in practice when
# the correlation is very high
R_illus <- chol(sigma_illus, pivot = TRUE)
R_illus <- R_illus[, order(attr(R_illus, "pivot"))]

# Multivariate normal draws. inverse-transform sampling using chol method:
rng_illus <- matrix(runif(n_illus * ncol(sigma_illus)), nrow = n_illus)

# NOTE: using qnorm() with uniform draws only is standard normal draws.
draws_illus <- qnorm(rng_illus) %*% R_illus
result_illus <- sweep(draws_illus, 2, mu_illus, "+")

# test that the means and correlations of the output draws are close to the
# inputs (Monte Carlo error means they will not be exact, hence a tolerance).
# Note you can drop rng now, or keep for auditing/QC later. Recommend to make
# this an option in your function(s) in your model.
max(abs(colMeans(result_illus) - mu_illus)) < 0.1
max(abs(stats::cor(result_illus) - sigma_illus)) < 0.1

# As a simple function you can use for most cases:
#' A simple function to perform inverse-transform sampling for multivariate
#' normal draws using the chol method.
#'
#' @param rng matrix of columns equal to length of params, and rows for number
#' of draws
#' @param params the (named) vector of mean values (e.g. regression
#' coefficients)
#' @param vcov variance-covariance matrix for the parameters (e.g. regression
#' coefficients). Must have dimnames matching `names(params)`.
#' @param R optional: pre-calculated chol of vcov (to save time if doing many
#' draws). Provide exactly one of `vcov` or `R`.
#'
#'
mvnorm_draws <- function(rng, params, vcov = NULL, R = NULL) {
  # you have to provide one of vcov or R, but not both.
  stopifnot(xor(is.null(vcov), is.null(R)))

  # params must be named because we don't want to lose track:
  stopifnot(
    !is.null(names(params)),
    all(nzchar(names(params)))
  )

  # optional: pre-calculated chol or do it here. If vcov given, its
  # dimnames must match params in order so that nothing is silently
  # misaligned. NOTE: `colnames(vcov) == names(params)` would be logical(0)
  # when vcov has no dimnames, and stopifnot(logical(0)) passes, so use
  # identical() instead.
  if (is.null(R)) {
    stopifnot(
      is.matrix(vcov),
      identical(colnames(vcov), names(params)),
      identical(rownames(vcov), names(params))
    )
    R <- chol(vcov, pivot = TRUE)
    R <- R[, order(attr(R, "pivot"))]
  }

  # validation checks:
  stopifnot(ncol(R) == length(params))
  stopifnot(ncol(rng) == length(params))
  stopifnot(nrow(rng) > 0)

  # draws using our uniform values for repeatability:
  draws <- qnorm(rng) %*% R
  out <- sweep(draws, 2, params, "+")
  colnames(out) <- names(params)
  out
}
```

4. Now that you have parametric model parameters for every PSA iteration, you
   can pass them to the appropriate functions *for (cumulative) hazards*, and
**not for survival**. For example, for simple `flexsurv` models there are
in-built functions for this already. (e.g. exponential hazard:
`flexsurv::hexp()`, exponential cumulative hazard: `flexsurv::Hexp()`). You can
use these to calculate transition probabilities for each model cycle that sum to
1, and correspond to each other for the different states. Note that this often
needs an "additive hazards" assumption, such that on the hazard scale
transitions add up. Difference in cumulative hazard between two time points:

Transitions add up. For each destination state $k$, the change in cumulative
hazard over model cycle $t$ (i.e. the interval $[t-1, t)$) is:

$$
\Delta H_k(t) = H_k(t) - H_k(t-1)
$$

The probability of leaving the current state during cycle $t$ uses the *total*
cumulative hazard across all destinations:

$$
p_{\text{exit}}(t) = 1 - \exp\left(-\sum_{j} \Delta H_j(t)\right)
$$

This is then shared between destinations in proportion to each one's cumulative
hazard:

$$
p_k(t) = \frac{\Delta H_k(t)}{\sum_{j} \Delta H_j(t)} \, p_{\text{exit}}(t)
$$

The probability of staying is $1 - p_{\text{exit}}(t)$, which `treatseqr`
computes for you. Hazards add, probabilities do not: converting each destination
separately as $1 - \exp(-\Delta H_k(t))$ and summing overstates the exits and
can exceed 1.


```{r time_units}
# NOTE: be very careful here about the time unit of the analysis and the time
# unit of the model! hazards are in continuous time, and transition
# probabilities are in discrete time. This means you need to align

# days in an average year takes leap years into account
days_in_a_year <- 365.25

# let's say the time unit of the survival analysis is months (days in an average
# month are 30.44)
tuota <- 30.44 / days_in_a_year

# but the CE model is in weeks.
cl <- 7 / days_in_a_year
```


```{r prob_probs_function}
# H_list: named list of cumulative hazard vectors (length n + 1, starting at t = 0),
# one per destination. Returns an n x K matrix of competing-risk TPs.
cum_haz_to_tps <- function(H_list) {
  H_mat <- do.call(cbind, H_list) # (n+1) x K, keeps destination names
  dH <- diff(H_mat)
  total <- rowSums(dH)
  p_exit <- 1 - exp(-total)
  dH * ifelse(total > 0, p_exit / total, 0)
}


#' Convert cumulative hazards to competing-risk transition probabilities
#'
#' Evaluates each destination's cumulative hazard at the model's cycle
#' boundaries, then converts the per-cycle increments to transition
#' probabilities. The probability of leaving the state uses the total hazard
#' across all destinations, and is shared between destinations in proportion
#' to each one's hazard increment. This is exact when the hazards are
#' proportional within a cycle.
#'
#' @param cum_hazards named list of cumulative hazard functions, one per
#'   destination state. Each takes a vector of times in the survival model's
#'   time unit and returns H(t), e.g.
#'   `function(t) flexsurv::Hweibull(t, shape, scale)`.
#' @param n_cycles number of model cycles to evaluate (`th` for pre-tunnel
#'   states, the tunnel length for tunnel states).
#' @param tuota time unit of the survival analysis, in years.
#' @param cl cycle length of the model, in years.
#'
#' @return `n_cycles` x K matrix of transition probabilities (one column per
#'   destination, named as in `cum_hazards`). Rows sum to the probability of
#'   exiting the state; `treatseqr` computes the probability of staying.
# get_prob_tps() then becomes a thin wrapper, so the existing test still holds
get_prob_tps <- function(cum_hazards, n_cycles, tuota, cl) {
  times <- seq.int(0, n_cycles) * cl / tuota
  cum_haz_to_tps(lapply(cum_hazards, function(H) H(times)))
}

# quick test:
p <- get_prob_tps(
  list(die = function(t) flexsurv::Hexp(t, rate = 0.1)),
  n_cycles = 5,
  tuota = tuota,
  cl = cl
)
all.equal(p[, "die"], rep(1 - exp(-0.1 * cl / tuota), 5))
```

The reason we are writing these ourself is important here. There is a function
`flexsurv::pmatrix.simfs()` which can use multi-state modelling for this, but it
is slow and over the course of many PSA draws it becomes unruly. This is a very
close approximation even if the shape of the distributions is different per exit
point (e.g. exponential for state 1 to 2 but Weibull for state 1 to 3). Beware
of censoring rules here as it is very important you are not double-counting
events!

As an example, you cannot just use PFS from the starting health state in an
oncology setting for the transition from progression free to the 2nd living
state (let's say 2nd line treatment). The hazard must be specifically for that
transition, meaning that the KM must be censored for everything else (death,
going to any other health state e.g. the patient has determined they do not want
any more treatment so has moved to a supportive care or no-treatment state and
the end of the pathway). This is very important as if you do not do this, you
will overestimate the rate at which patients leave progression-free, and send
some to second line who should have died. In this example, the appropriate
endpoint would be time to second line therapy, so it is less complicated than it
sounds!

## Usual expectation of stats output

Usually, the output from statistics will be parameters and variance-covariance.
For this example, we will emulate that with some of the more simple
distributions (exponential and Weibull). Once you have selected the best fitting
distributions for your base case and want to vary them in the PSA, you would
organise the parameters in the same way structurally as the TP data in our
deterministic examples.

### A note about scales

`flexsurv` estimates its models on a *transformed* scale (for example
`log(rate)`, `log(shape)`, `log(scale)`), and that is the scale which
`coef(fit)` and `vcov(fit)` are produced. The multivariate normal is only
appropriate on that same scale. Drawing `rate` or `shape` directly could give
you the wrong numbers. So the structure below stores `coefs` and `vcov` exactly
as `flexsurv` returns them, and the inverse transforms (which `flexsurv` exposes
per distribution in `flexsurv::flexsurv.dists[[dist]]$inv.transforms`) are
applied *after* the draw to recover the natural-scale parameters that the hazard
functions expect. With a real fit, `coefs = coef(fit)` and `vcov = vcov(fit)` is
all you need. Note also that the off-diagonal elements of `vcov` are rarely zero
in practice (log-shape and log-scale of a Weibull are usually strongly
correlated), so the Weibull examples below carry a non-zero covariance:

```{r stats_output}
# small helper so every vcov includes parameter names. x is the vector of
# standard errors on the transformed scale, and rho the correlation (used for
# the 2-parameter distributions only).
named_vcov <- function(se, nms, rho = 0) {
  stopifnot(length(se) == length(nms))
  cor_mat <- matrix(rho, nrow = length(nms), ncol = length(nms))
  diag(cor_mat) <- 1
  m <- outer(se, se) * cor_mat
  dimnames(m) <- list(nms, nms)
  m
}

flexsurv_output <- list(
  on_trt = list(
    surgery = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.05)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.10, "rate")
    ),
    die = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.01)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.20, "rate")
    )
  ),
  surgery = list(
    failed_surg = list(
      dist = "weibull",
      coefs = c(shape = log(1.5), scale = log(3)),
      vcov = named_vcov(c(0.07, 0.07), c("shape", "scale"), rho = -0.3)
    ),
    responder = list(
      dist = "weibull",
      coefs = c(shape = log(1.2), scale = log(5)),
      vcov = named_vcov(c(0.10, 0.10), c("shape", "scale"), rho = -0.3)
    ),
    die = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.05)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.10, "rate")
    )
  ),
  responder = list(
    palliative = list(
      dist = "weibull",
      coefs = c(shape = log(1.1), scale = log(7)),
      vcov = named_vcov(c(0.12, 0.12), c("shape", "scale"), rho = -0.3)
    ),
    die = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.01)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.20, "rate")
    )
  ),
  failed_surg = list(
    # NOTE: exponential on purpose, see "Fixed-duration tunnels" below
    palliative = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.27)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.15, "rate")
    ),
    die = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.02)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.15, "rate")
    )
  ),
  palliative = list(
    die = list(
      dist = "exp",
      coefs = c(rate = log(0.25)),
      vcov = named_vcov(0.04, "rate")
    )
  )
)
```

## Fixed-duration tunnels, decision nodes, and holding states

Survival-driven hazards describe the *time-to-event* transitions. They do not
reproduce the two fixed-duration structures from `fixed-duration-tunnels.Rmd`,
and it is easy to get this wrong:

- `surgery` is a 3-cycle tunnel with a **decision-tree node** at `d = 3`: every
  patient leaves at the end of the tunnel, split between `failed_surg`,
  `responder` and `die`. A cumulative-hazard extrapolation evaluated at
  `d = 1, 2, 3` gives a small exit probability at each cycle and a large
  `p_stay` at `d = 3`. `treatseqr` then treats `d = 3` as a holding state and
  re-applies the week-3 hazard increment forever, which is not the model we
  want. The node has to be imposed explicitly on the last cycle.
- `failed_surg` is a 2-cycle tunnel with a **holding state** at `d = 2`: the
  `d = 2` transition probabilities are re-applied every subsequent cycle. That is
  a constant-hazard (exponential) extrapolation from the end of the tunnel, so
  the hazard feeding it should be constant too. Freezing the week-2 increment of
  a Weibull with a rising hazard would quietly understate exits for the rest of
  the horizon. This is why `failed_surg -> palliative` is specified as `exp`
  above.

For the node we need a probabilistic split that always sums to 1. The natural
choice is a Dirichlet distribution, parameterised as pseudo-counts (here the
`0.35 / 0.55 / 0.10` split from the deterministic vignette, as if observed in
100 patients). A Dirichlet draw is a set of independent gamma draws normalised
to sum to 1, so it can use the same uniform streams as everything else:

```{r node_output}
node_output <- list(
  surgery = c(failed_surg = 35, responder = 55, die = 10)
)
```

If you can arrange the parameters and variance-covariance matrices in this way,
you can then use a function to produce "blocks" of transitions, with one column
per iteration of the PSA. `R` is "column-major" so the columns are the
iterations and the rows are the cycles, as it would be very slow to do it the
other way around. 

Because `R` is vectorised, drawing in this way is very fast and efficient, and
you can use the same random number stream for each PSA. Essentially, you
pre-draw all the parameters in one go for all the PSA iterations, and then
individually use them to do the extrapolation for each. This prevents the model
from using a lot of memory from storing all transition probabilities for all
iterations at once.

It helps to draw the uniforms in a local scope so the global random number
generator is left as you found it. Otherwise `set.seed()` somewhere else in the
model means something different depending on whether the PSA draws have run or
not. Second, every uniform stream should have a name
(`state.destination.parameter`) and, these should be looked it up by name
rather than by column position. If you later add a transition, or want to
compare two scenarios with common random numbers, the streams feeding the
transitions you did not touch stay exactly the same. You can also keep the named
`rng` matrix for auditing, and pass it back in via the `rng` argument.

```{r draw_params}
# Map the draws from flexsurv's estimation scale back to the natural scale
# the H*() functions expect. flexsurv.dists records, per distribution, the
# parameter names (in order) and the inverse transform for each one, so we
# don't have to maintain a table of which parameters are logged.
flexsurv_inv_transform <- function(draws, dist) {
  dists <- flexsurv::flexsurv.dists
  key <- match(tolower(dist), tolower(names(dists)))
  stopifnot(!is.na(key))
  dinfo <- dists[[key]]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(draws), dinfo$pars))
  for (j in seq_along(dinfo$pars)) {
    draws[, j] <- dinfo$inv.transforms[[j]](draws[, j])
  }
  draws
}

# Draw the uniform streams for every parameter in one go, without disturbing
# the global RNG state: set.seed() elsewhere in your model will behave the same
# whether or not this function has been called. Columns are named
# state.destination.parameter so each stream can be identified later.
draw_uniforms <- function(n_draws, stream_names, seed) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(seed), length(seed) == 1)
  has_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  old_seed <- if (has_seed) get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
  on.exit({
    if (has_seed) {
      assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = globalenv())
    } else {
      rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
    }
  })
  set.seed(seed)
  matrix(
    runif(n_draws * length(stream_names)),
    nrow = n_draws,
    dimnames = list(NULL, stream_names)
  )
}

draw_params <- function(flexsurv_output, n_draws, rng = NULL, seed = NULL) {
  # give exactly one of the seed or the pre-drawn rng
  stopifnot(xor(is.null(seed), is.null(rng)))

  # uniform draws named state.destination.parameter per parameter. The
  # streams are looked up by name.
  stream_names <- unlist(lapply(names(flexsurv_output), function(state_name) {
    state <- flexsurv_output[[state_name]]
    lapply(names(state), function(dest_name) {
      paste(state_name, dest_name, names(state[[dest_name]]$coefs), sep = ".")
    })
  }))

  if (is.null(rng)) {
    rng <- draw_uniforms(n_draws, stream_names, seed)
  }
  stopifnot(
    is.matrix(rng),
    nrow(rng) == n_draws,
    all(stream_names %in% colnames(rng))
  )

  # cycle through states then destinations, pulling each destination's streams
  # out of rng by name, drawing on the estimation scale, then transforming back.
  #
  # because R is column-major, we transpose the output.
  # This code is the crux so take your time reading it.
  Map(function(state, state_name) {
    Map(function(dest, dest_name) {
      cols <- paste(state_name, dest_name, names(dest$coefs), sep = ".")
      draws <- mvnorm_draws(
        rng[, cols, drop = FALSE],
        dest$coefs,
        vcov = dest$vcov
      )
      list(
        dist = dest$dist,
        params = t(flexsurv_inv_transform(draws, dest$dist))
      )
    }, state, names(state))
  }, flexsurv_output, names(flexsurv_output))
}

# because of column-major (columns faster than rows) in R, for each PSA we pull
# out a column from the parameter set:

n_psa <- 1000
prob_params <- draw_params(
  flexsurv_output = flexsurv_output,
  n_draws = n_psa,
  seed = 12345
)
str(prob_params)

# The draws are now on the natural scale, so rates and shapes are strictly
# positive even in the tails:
range(prob_params$on_trt$die$params)
range(prob_params$surgery$failed_surg$params["shape", ])
```

The decision-node splits are drawn in the same way, one Dirichlet per node,
with streams named `state.node.destination`. Each state's draws come back as a
`destinations x n_draws` matrix so they can be indexed by iteration exactly like
the survival parameters:

```{r draw_nodes}
draw_nodes <- function(node_output, n_draws, rng = NULL, seed = NULL) {
  stopifnot(xor(is.null(seed), is.null(rng)))

  stream_names <- unlist(lapply(names(node_output), function(state_name) {
    paste(state_name, "node", names(node_output[[state_name]]), sep = ".")
  }))

  if (is.null(rng)) {
    rng <- draw_uniforms(n_draws, stream_names, seed)
  }
  stopifnot(
    is.matrix(rng),
    nrow(rng) == n_draws,
    all(stream_names %in% colnames(rng))
  )

  Map(function(alpha, state_name) {
    cols <- paste(state_name, "node", names(alpha), sep = ".")
    # Dirichlet(alpha) = independent Gamma(alpha_k, 1) draws, normalised.
    # qgamma() on the uniform streams keeps this fully reproducible.
    g <- qgamma(rng[, cols, drop = FALSE], shape = rep(alpha, each = n_draws))
    g <- g / rowSums(g)
    out <- t(g)
    dimnames(out) <- list(names(alpha), NULL)
    out
  }, node_output, names(node_output))
}

node_params <- draw_nodes(node_output, n_draws = n_psa, seed = 54321)
str(node_params)

# centred on the deterministic split, and every column sums to 1:
round(rowMeans(node_params$surgery), 3)
all(abs(colSums(node_params$surgery) - 1) < 1e-12)
```

Now we have parametric survival modelling parameters for every state, in the
original TUoTA (time unit of the analysis) and cycle length (CL) of the model,
plus a draw for each decision node. When we perform the PSA, we can then follow
a set process from this point onwards:

1. Pull out the parameters (and node splits) for a given iteration of the PSA
2. Use parameters the distribution name to extrapolate the cumulative hazard for
   each destination state
3. Use those to compute the transition probabilities for each cycle of the
   model, using the `get_prob_tps()` function defined above.
4. For any state with a decision node, overwrite the last cycle of its tunnel
   with the node split (so `p_stay = 0` there).
5. Compute `p_stay` as `1 - p_exit` and populate the transition probability matrix for
   that iteration of the PSA.
6. Validate the transition probability matrix for that iteration of the PSA, and
   then run the model for that iteration, storing the consolidated trace for
that iteration.

```{r psa_set_up}
get_params_psa <- function(prob_params, iter) {
  rapply(
    prob_params,
    function(m) m[, iter],
    classes = "matrix",
    how = "replace"
  )
}
str(get_params_psa(prob_params, 1))
# example: for iteration 1, the shape and scale for surgery to responder, and
# the node split at the end of the surgery tunnel:
get_params_psa(prob_params, 1)$surgery$responder$params
get_params_psa(node_params, 1)$surgery
```

Now we can use a "router" for the method to get the cumulative hazard:


```{r get_cum_haz_func}
# router to the method to get cumulative hazard for each distribution. Downside
# is you need to know what to put in each function!
route_method_cum_haz <- function(dist) {
  switch(tolower(dist),
    exp = flexsurv::Hexp, # rate
    exponential = flexsurv::Hexp, # rate
    weibull = flexsurv::Hweibull, # shape, scale (AFT)
    weibullph = flexsurv::HweibullPH, # shape, scale (PH)
    gompertz = flexsurv::Hgompertz, # shape, rate
    lnorm = flexsurv::Hlnorm, # meanlog, sdlog
    llogis = flexsurv::Hllogis, # shape, scale
    gamma = flexsurv::Hgamma, # shape, rate
    gengamma = flexsurv::Hgengamma, # mu, sigma, Q
    genf = flexsurv::Hgenf, # mu, sigma, Q, P. rarely used
    stop("Unsupported distribution: '", dist, "'")
  )
}
# for example, get the weibull method and give me the first year:
route_method_cum_haz("weibull")(
  x = 0:52 * (7 / 365.25),
  shape = 1.5,
  scale = 3
) |> round(2)
```

Because we have the string to go in there for all of our parameter sets, we can
automatically cycle through the states and destinations to get the cumulative
hazard functions for each destination state. We can then use those to compute
the transition probabilities for each cycle of the model.

```{r cumulative_hazards}
generate_cum_haz <- function(time_points, params) {
  lapply(params, function(state) {
    lapply(state, function(dest) {
      H_func <- route_method_cum_haz(dest$dist)
      do.call(
        H_func,
        c(list(time_points), as.list(dest$params))
      )
    })
  })
}
time_points <- seq.int(0, th) * cl / tuota
# finally, we arrive at the cumulative hazard for each trasision we have data
# for:
cum_hazards <- generate_cum_haz(
  time_points = time_points,
  params = get_params_psa(prob_params, 1)
)
```

Now that we have the cumulative hazards, we can get the transition probabilities
for this PSA iteration. This means we can start to connect everything up!


```{r psa_setup_full}
n_cycles <- c(
  on_trt = th,
  responder = th,
  surgery = 3L,
  failed_surg = 2L,
  palliative = th
)

# make sure the states are ordered in the right way
state_names <- c(
  "on_trt",
  "surgery",
  "failed_surg",
  "responder",
  "palliative",
  "die"
)

# Turn one iteration's cumulative hazards (and node splits) into a tp_source
# list in the order treatseqr expects.
build_tp_source <- function(cum_haz_i, nodes_i, n_cycles, state_names) {
  tp_source_i <- Map(function(state, n) {
    tp <- cum_haz_to_tps(state)[seq_len(n), , drop = FALSE]
    as.list(as.data.frame(tp))
  }, cum_haz_i, n_cycles[names(cum_haz_i)])

  for (state_name in names(nodes_i)) {
    split <- nodes_i[[state_name]]
    n <- n_cycles[[state_name]]
    tp_state <- tp_source_i[[state_name]]
    for (dest_name in union(names(tp_state), names(split))) {
      if (is.null(tp_state[[dest_name]])) tp_state[[dest_name]] <- numeric(n)
      tp_state[[dest_name]][n] <- if (dest_name %in% names(split)) {
        split[[dest_name]]
      } else {
        0
      }
    }
    tp_source_i[[state_name]] <- tp_state
  }

  tp_source_i[setdiff(state_names, "die")]
}

psa_iteration <- 1
cum_haz_i <- generate_cum_haz(
  time_points,
  get_params_psa(prob_params, psa_iteration)
)
tp_source_i <- build_tp_source(
  cum_haz_i,
  get_params_psa(node_params, psa_iteration),
  n_cycles,
  state_names
)

# validate the TPs:
valid_tp_i <- validate_tp_source(
  tp_source_i,
  tunnel_lengths = c(3L, 2L, th, th)
)

# the surgery tunnel has p_stay = 0 at d = 3 (the decision node), and the
# holding state at the end of failed_surg has a constant exit probability:
round(1 - Reduce(`+`, valid_tp_i$surgery), 3)
round(1 - Reduce(`+`, valid_tp_i$failed_surg), 3)

# compile m
mlist <- generate_m_list(
  m_specification = m_spec,
  transition_prob_list = valid_tp_i,
  state_names = state_names
)

# extrapolate trace
trace <- extrapolate_treatseqr(m = mlist, spec = m_spec)
consol <- treatseqr::consolidate_treatseqr_trace(trace, m_spec, state_names)
matplot(
  consol[["t"]][, setdiff(state_names, "die")],
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  col = seq_along(state_names),
  xlab = "Cycle",
  ylab = "Proportion of cohort"
)
```



## Bringing it all together

Now that we've done all that, we can populate a 3d array with the probabilistic
trace:

```{r psa_runner}
run_psa_iteration <- function(
  time_points,
  prob_params,
  node_params,
  n_cycles,
  state_names,
  th,
  iter,
  m_spec
) {
  cum_haz_i <- generate_cum_haz(time_points, get_params_psa(prob_params, iter))
  tp_source_i <- build_tp_source(
    cum_haz_i,
    get_params_psa(node_params, iter),
    n_cycles,
    state_names
  )

  valid_tp_i <- validate_tp_source(
    tp_source_i,
    tunnel_lengths = c(3L, 2L, th, th)
  )
  m_i <- generate_m_list(m_spec, valid_tp_i, state_names = state_names)
  trace_i <- extrapolate_treatseqr(m = m_i, spec = m_spec)
  consolidate_treatseqr_trace(
    trace_i,
    m_spec,
    state_names
  )
}


# run iteration 1:
head(run_psa_iteration(
  time_points,
  prob_params,
  node_params,
  n_cycles,
  state_names,
  th,
  iter = 1,
  m_spec
)$t, 2)

# run the psa:
psa_output <- vapply(
  seq_len(n_psa),
  function(iter) {
    run_psa_iteration(
      time_points,
      prob_params,
      node_params,
      n_cycles,
      state_names,
      th,
      iter,
      m_spec
    )$t
  },
  matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = th + 1,
    ncol = length(state_names)
  )
)
```

The above is your trace for all of the PSA iterations. You can use this to
compute your cost-effectiveness outputs like this in one go, or can compute them
on the iteration level by manipulating the function . This could dramatically
reduce the amount of data coming out of the model (as the trace is the biggest
object typically and for PSA you usually only need top-level outputs).

Fully integrating the treatseqr engine into your model's PSA is up to you, but
this example is likely to be very flexible and essentially applies to any model.
